strengths: Technically sound proofs with sophisticated techniques (especially Lemma 3.2's clever partitioning argument and Theorem 2.15's case analysis)
Answers multiple open questions from prior work (Raman & Raman 2025), including the first characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generation
Surprising equivalence result (Theorem 2.14): all noise levels i ≥ 1 are equivalent, contrasting with strict hierarchy in related setting
Simplified characterizations (NC₁(C) < ∞ replacing NCᵢ(C) < ∞ for all i) are more elegant than prior work
Clear presentation with formal definitions, logical progression, and comprehensive treatment of both uniform and non-uniform cases
weaknesses: Overstated motivation: Introduction claims relevance to understanding LLMs and hallucinations, but the abstract formal framework bears little resemblance to practical language models (no semantics, efficiency, or realistic noise patterns)
Limited practical significance: Results are specialized to a narrow theoretical framework with minimal implications for real LLM robustness or practical machine learning

Insufficient intuition for key results: Why are noise levels 1, 2, 3... equivalent when 0 and 1 are separated? Why does equivalence hold for uniform/non-uniform generation but not generation in the limit? These questions lack explanation

Theorem 2.15 construction introduced without motivation: Algorithm 1 appears mid-proof; the intuition for the 'column' construction and why it works should be explained upfront, not buried in technical details

Incremental within established framework: The paper refines existing notions (noise-level generatability, noise-dependent generation) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts; once these definitions exist, equivalence questions follow naturally
Missing technical discussion: No treatment of computational complexity (is NC₁(C) < ∞ decidable?), tightness of Lemma 3.2's square-root bound, or why the threshold at noise level 1 is special
Limited concrete examples: No explicit examples of collections with specific NC₁(C) values; the separation in Theorem 2.15 remains abstract
Framework limitations underexplored: Assumptions (countable collections, infinite languages, non-repeating enumerations) and their practical implications not discussed

strengths: Resolves multiple open questions from recent work (Raman & Raman 2025), particularly regarding separation between noiseless and noisy generation and the first characterization of non-uniform noise-dependent generation
Presents surprising and non-obvious theoretical results: the equivalence between noise level 1 and any level i≥1 sharply contrasts with the infinite hierarchy in prior work (Bai et al. 2026)
Lemma 3.2 provides clever technical insight relating NC_{i-1}(C) to √(NC_i(C)) using clever partitioning and closure arguments
Simplifies existing characterizations: reduces the noise-dependent generation characterization from requiring NC_i(C) < ∞ for all i to just NC_1(C) < ∞
Well-organized presentation with clear definitions and logical progression through uniform and non-uniform cases; all definitions and results are clearly stated
Comprehensive treatment covering both uniform and non-uniform variants and both noise-level and noise-dependent formulations
weaknesses: Limited practical relevance: despite framing around LLMs and hallucinations, the formal model is far removed from practical concerns. The framework ignores statistical properties, computational complexity, and doesn't provide actionable insights for language model design

Largely incremental contributions: all results fundamentally follow from the equivalence NC_1(C) < ∞ ⟺ NC_i(C) < ∞ for i≥1; remaining results are relatively straightforward applications via standard constructions (Lemma 4.1)
Techniques are relatively standard: beyond Lemma 3.2, proofs rely on well-known partitioning, closure manipulations, and pigeonhole arguments with no novel algorithmic or analytical insights

The separation result in Theorem 2.17 uses an artificial construction (N×N universe with column-based languages) that appears designed specifically to make the proof work rather than arising naturally from the problem
Insufficient intuition for key results: why does a single noisy string fundamentally break generatability? The paper lacks clear conceptual explanation beyond technical arguments
Missing discussion of tightness, intermediate notions, or practical algorithmic implications; complex characterizations (e.g., countable unions in Theorem 2.19) lack intuition
Algorithm 1 in Theorem 2.17 proof is somewhat informal; the complex condition on line 5 could be clearer
